MS. ALVINA LOPES

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 2

Recovery System: Recovery Concepts
• A computer system, like any other device, is subject to failure.
• Therefore, the database system must take actions in advance to ensure that the atomicity and 
durability properties of transactions are preserved.
• A recovery system ensures that the database remains consistent and correct even after failures 
like:
• System crash 
• Power failure 
• Transaction errors 
• The recovery scheme must also support high availability. 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 3

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 4
1. Transaction
•A sequence of operations 
(Read/Write) 
•Must follow ACID properties
2. Commit
•Transaction successfully completed
Changes are permanently saved
3. Abort (Rollback)
•Transaction fails
All changes are undone
4. Failure Types
•Transaction failure → logical error 
•System crash → power/OS failure 
•Disk failure → hardware issue 
5. Stable Storage
•Storage that never loses data (ideal 
concept)
•Used to store logs safely 
Basic Recovery Concepts

Failure Classification
•Transaction failure :
• Logical errors: transaction cannot complete due to some internal error condition
• System errors: the database system must terminate an active transaction due to an 
error condition (e.g., deadlock)
•System crash: a power failure or other hardware or software failure causes the system to 
crash.
• Fail-stop assumption: non-volatile storage contents are assumed to not be 
corrupted by system crash
• Database systems have numerous integrity checks to prevent corruption of disk data
•Disk failure: a head crash or similar disk failure destroys all or part of disk storage
• Destruction is assumed to be detectable: disk drives use checksums to detect 
failures
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 5

Failure Classification
Recovery Algorithms
• Recovery algorithms are techniques to ensure database consistency and 
transaction atomicity and durability despite failures
• Recovery algorithms have two parts
1. Actions taken during normal transaction processing to ensure enough 
information exists to recover from failures
2. Actions taken after a failure to recover the database contents to a state that 
ensures atomicity, consistency and durability
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 6

Storage Structure
•Volatile storage:
• does not survive system crashes
• examples: main memory, cache memory
•Nonvolatile storage:
• survives system crashes
• examples: disk, tape, flash memory, non-volatile (battery backed up) RAM
•Stable storage:
• a mythical form of storage that survives all failures
• approximated by maintaining multiple copies on distinct nonvolatile media
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 7

Stable Storage Implementation
• To implement stable storage, we need to 
1. replicate the needed information in several non-volatile storage media (usually disk) 
with independent failure modes and 
2. update the information in a controlled manner 
to ensure that failure during data transfer does not damage the needed information.
• Maintain multiple copies of each block on separate disks
• copies can be at remote sites to protect against disasters such as fire or flooding.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 8

Stable Storage Implementation
•Failure during data transfer can still result in inconsistent copies: Block transfer can 
result in
• Successful completion
• Partial failure: destination block has incorrect information
• Total failure: destination block was never updated
•Protecting storage media from failure during data transfer (one solution):
• Execute output operation as follows (assuming two copies of each block):
1. Write the information onto the first physical block.
2. When the first write successfully completes, write the same information onto the second physical 
block.
3. The output is completed only after the second write successfully completes.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 9

Stable Storage Implementation
•Protecting storage media from failure during data transfer:
•Copies of a block may differ due to failure during output operation. To recover from failure:
•1. First find inconsistent blocks:
1. Expensive solution: Compare the two copies of every disk block.
2. Better solution:
Record in-progress disk writes on non-volatile storage (Nonvolatile RAM or special area of disk).
Use this information during recovery to find blocks that may be inconsistent, and only compare 
copies of these.
Used in hardware RAID systems
•2. If either copy of an inconsistent block is detected to have an error (bad checksum), 
overwrite it by the other copy. If both have no error, but are different, overwrite the second 
block by the first block. 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 10

Data Access
•Physical blocks are those blocks residing on the disk.
•Buffer blocks are the blocks residing temporarily in main memory.
•Block movements between disk and main memory are initiated through the 
following two operations:
• input(B) transfers the physical block B to main memory.
• output(B) transfers the buffer block B to the disk, and replaces the appropriate 
physical block there.
•We assume, for simplicity, that each data item fits in, and is stored inside, a single 
block.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 11

Data Access
• Each transaction Ti has its private work-area in which local copies of all data items accessed 
and updated by it are kept.
• Ti 's local copy of a data item X is called xi.
•Transferring data items between system buffer blocks and its private work-area done by:
• read(X) assigns the value of data item X to the local variable xi.
• write(X) assigns the value of local variable xi to data item {X} in the buffer block.
• Note: output(BX) need not immediately follow write(X). System can perform the output operation 
when it deems fit.
•Transactions
• Must perform read(X) before accessing X for the first time (subsequent reads can be from local copy).
• write(X) can be executed at any time before the transaction commits.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 12

Data Access
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 13
Figure 1. Block storage operations.

Recovery and Atomicity
• To ensure atomicity despite failures, we first output information describing the 
modifications to stable storage without modifying the database itself.
• 2 techniques:
1. Log-based recovery
2. Shadow-paging 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 14

Recovery Techniques
1. Log-Based Recovery
Uses logs to Undo/Redo operations
Two types: 
◦ Deferred Update (Redo only) 
◦ Immediate Update (Undo + Redo) 
2. Shadow Paging
Maintains old and new page copies
No need for logs 
Recovery by switching page tables
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 15

Shadow Paging
•Shadow Paging is alternative to log-based recovery.
•This scheme is useful if transactions execute serially. 
•It ensures ACID properties (atomicity and durability) without using logs
•It maintains two page tables.
1. Shadow Page Table (original, stable state) 
2. Current Page Table (for active updates). 
•Updates are made on a new copy, not on the original.
•It enables fast, instantaneous recovery by discarding the current table upon 
failure and switching tables upon commit.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 16

Shadow Paging
•Store the shadow page table in nonvolatile storage, such that state of the database 
prior to transaction execution may be recovered.
• Shadow page table is never modified during execution.
•To start with, both the page tables are identical. 
•Only current page table is used for data item accesses during execution of the 
transaction. 
•Whenever any page is about to be written for the first time
• A copy of this page is made onto an unused page.
• The current page table is then made to point to the copy
• The update is performed on the copy
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 17

Shadow Paging
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 18

Shadow Paging
Key Components and Working:
•Two Tables: When a transaction starts, the current page table is a copy of the 
shadow page table. Both point to the same pages on the disk.
•Out-of-Place Updates: When a page is modified, a new block is allocated on the 
disk, and the modification is written there. The current page table points to this 
new block, while the shadow page table still points to the old, unmodified block.
•Commit: To commit, the current page table becomes the new shadow page table, 
and the old disk blocks are freed.
•Abort/Recovery: If the transaction fails, the current page table is discarded, and 
the shadow table remains, effectively reversing changes without undo operations.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 19

Shadow Paging
Advantages:
Fast Recovery: No UNDO or REDO operations are required.
No Overhead: Eliminates the need for writing log records to the disk continuously. 
Disadvantages:
Data Fragmentation: Pages become scattered on the disk over time, reducing 
performance.
High Commit Cost: Committing requires updating the entire page table and clearing old 
pages, which is inefficient.
Concurrency Issues: Difficult to manage multiple concurrent transactions compared to 
log-based techniques
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 20

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 21
2. Current Directory 
This is the working copy
It points to: 
Some old pages
Some new updated pages
Example:
Page 2 → now points to Page 2 (new)
Page 5 → now points to Page 5 (new)
3. Middle Section (Pages)
we can see:
•Page 2 (old) and Page 2 (new) 
•Page 5 (old) and Page 5 (new) 
•Old pages are unchanged
•New pages are modified copies

Shadow Paging
Working of Shadow Paging 
Initial State
System maintains a page table called Shadow Directory
A Current Directory is created as a copy of shadow directory 
Both directories point to same data pages initially
When Transaction Starts
A new Current Directory is used for updates 
Shadow Directory remains unchanged (safe backup)
Both directories still point to same pages at start
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 22

Shadow Paging
When a Page is Updated
System does NOT modify original page
A new copy of the page is created
Example from diagram: 
◦ Page 2 (old) → Page 2 (new) 
◦ Page 5 (old) → Page 5 (new) 
Updating the Current Directory
Current directory pointers are updated to new pages
Unchanged pages still point to old pages
So current directory has mix of old + new pages
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 23

Shadow Paging
Shadow Directory Behavior
Shadow directory remains unchanged
It continues to point to only old pages
Acts as a backup version of database
During Execution
Two versions exist: 
◦ Shadow version → old data
◦ Current version → updated data
All operations use current directory
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 24

Shadow Paging
Commit Operation
When transaction is successful: 
◦ Current directory becomes the new main directory
◦ Shadow directory is replaced
New pages become permanent
Abort / System Failure
If failure occurs before commit: 
◦ Current directory is discarded
◦ Shadow directory is used 
Database returns to previous consistent state
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 25

Log-Based Recovery
• Log is the most widely used structure for recording database modifications.
•A log is a sequence of log records.
•It records all the update activities in the database. 
•It is used to recover the database after a crash or failure. 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 26

Log-Based Recovery
Update Log Record (Structure)
Each log entry for a write operation contains:
•Transaction ID (Ti) → Which transaction performed the operation 
•Data Item (Xj) → Which data item was modified 
•Old Value (V1) → Value before the update 
•New Value (V2) → Value after the update 
Example:
<T1, X, 100, 150>
Transaction T1 changed X from 100 → 150
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 27

Log-Based Recovery
Types of Log Records
Start Record
◦ <Ti start> → Transaction Ti has started 
Write Record
◦ <Ti, Xj, V1, V2> 
◦ Shows update from old value to new value 
Commit Record
◦ <Ti commit> → Transaction completed successfully 
Abort Record
◦ <Ti abort> → Transaction failed and was rolled back
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 28

Log-Based Recovery
• When transaction Ti starts, it registers itself by writing a <Ti start> log record
• Before Ti executes write(X), a log record <Ti, X, V1, V2> is written.
• When Ti finishes it last statement, the log record <Ti commit> is written. 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 29

Log-Based Recovery
Two Log-Based Recovery Techniques
1. Deferred Database Modification (Lazy Update)
Changes are not applied immediately to the database 
Updates are stored in log first 
Applied only at commit
Recovery:
•Redo only committed transactions . No need to undo anything 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 30

Log-Based Recovery
Two Log-Based Recovery Techniques
2. Immediate Database Modification (Eager Update)
Allows updates of an uncommitted transaction to be made to the buffer, or the disk itself,
before the transaction commits
Changes are applied immediately to database
Log is written before actual update (Write-Ahead Logging)
Order in which blocks are output can be different from the order in which they are written.
Recovery:
•Undo uncommitted transactions . Redo committed transactions
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 31

Transaction Commit
• A transaction is said to have committed when its commit log record is output to 
stable storage
• All previous log records of the transaction must have been output already.
• Writes performed by a transaction may still be in the buffer when the transaction 
commits, and may be output later.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 32

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 33
Immediate Database Modification Example

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 34
•All updates are recorded in the log first
•Actual database write is delayed until the transaction 
commits 
•That’s why it’s called “deferred” (postponed)
First log → then commit → then update database
Step-by-Step Working
1. Transaction Starts
•Log entry:
•<Ti start>
2. Write Operation Occurs
•When write(X) happens:
•<Ti, X, V>
•Only new value (V) is stored
Old value is NOT needed
Deferred Database Modification (Lazy Update) 3. No Immediate Database Update
•The actual database is NOT changed yet
•Changes are just sitting in the log
4. Commit Happens
•Log entry:
•<Ti commit>
5. Apply Changes to Database
•After commit: 
• System reads log 
• Applies all recorded updates to database
Recovery Mechanism
If system crashes:
• Only REDO is needed
• Redo all transactions that have <commit> 
• Ignore incomplete transactions 
• No UNDO required

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 35
Example (Very Important)
Log:
<T1 start>
<T1, A, 500>
<T1, B, 300>
<T1 commit>
After crash:
Apply:
•A = 500 
•B = 300 
Advantages
•Simple recovery 
•No undo operation needed 
•Less complexity 
Disadvantages
•Updates delayed → slower response 
•Not suitable for real-time systems

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 36
•Database is updated immediately, even before the transaction 
commits 
•Unlike deferred, changes are directly written to database 
while transaction is active
•“Update now, commit later”
Key Rule 
Log must be written BEFORE database update
This is called: Write-Ahead Logging (WAL)
•First → write log to stable storage 
•Then → update database 
Ensures recovery is always possible
• Updates can be written: Before commit OR after commit
• Order of writing: May be different from execution order
• Logs are stored in stable storage
Immediate Database Modification Recovery Mechanism
After crash:
• If transaction is COMMITTED: REDO 
required
Reapply changes using new values 
• If transaction is NOT committed: UNDO 
required
Rollback using old values 
USE BOTH UNDO and REDO
Because:
• Some updates may already be written before 
crash 
• Some may not be written 
So system must:
• Undo incomplete work 
• Redo completed work

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 37
Working Steps
1. Transaction Starts
<Ti start>
2. Write Operation
<Ti, X, old value, new value>
Both values are stored:
•Old value → for UNDO 
•New value → for REDO 
3. Immediate Update
•Database is updated right away
•Even if transaction is not committed yet 
4. Commit
<Ti commit>
Example
Log:
<T1 start>
<T1, A, 100, 150>
<T1, B, 200, 250>
Crash happens (no commit)
Recovery:
•UNDO T1: 
• A → 100 
• B → 200 
Advantages
•Faster updates (no delay) 
•Suitable for real-time systems 
Disadvantages
•Complex recovery (UNDO + REDO needed) 
•Needs careful logging (WAL)

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 38
Feature Deferred Immediate
Update Time After commit Before commit
Log Stores New value only Old + New values
Recovery REDO only UNDO + REDO
Deferred Database Modification and Immediate Database Modification

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 39
Given Log (Before Crash)
Assume the system log is:
<T1 start>
<T1, A, 100, 150>
<T2 start>
<T2, B, 200, 250>
<T1, C, 300, 350>
<T1 commit>
<T2, D, 400, 450>
CRASH
Step 1: Identify Transaction States
Transaction Status
T1 Committed
T2 Not committed
Rule: Committed → REDO
Uncommitted → UNDO
Step 2: REDO Phase (Forward Direction ) 
Apply all changes of committed transactions (T1)
Operations of 
T1:<T1, A, 100, 150> → A = 150
<T1, C, 300, 350> → C = 350
After REDO: A = 150 and C = 350
Step 3: UNDO Phase (Backward Direction )
Undo all changes of uncommitted transactions (T2)
Go backwards in log Operations of 
T2:<T2, D, 400, 450> → D = 400 (undo)
<T2, B, 200, 250> → B = 200 (undo)
After UNDO: B = 200 and D = 400
• T1 changes are preserved (because committed)
• T2 changes are rolled back (because no commit)
Data Item Final Value
A 150
B 200
C 350
D 400
Immediate Database Modification.

Undo and Redo Operations
• undo(Ti) -- restores the value of all data items updated by Ti to their old values, 
going backwards from the last log record for Ti
• Each time a data item X is restored to its old value V a special log record <Ti , 
X, V> is written out
• When undo of a transaction is complete, a log record <Ti abort> is written out.
• redo(Ti) -- sets the value of all data items updated by Ti to the new values, going 
forward from the first log record for Ti
• No logging is done in this case.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 40

Recovering from Failure
• When recovering after failure:
• Transaction Ti needs to be undone if the log
• Contains the record <Ti start>,
• But does not contain either the record <Ti commit> or <Ti abort>.
• Transaction Ti needs to be redone if the log
• Contains the records <Ti start>
• And contains the record <Ti commit> or <Ti abort>
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 41

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 42
Immediate DB Modification Recovery Example

Checkpoints
• Redoing/undoing all transactions recorded in the log can be very slow
• Processing the entire log is time-consuming if the system has run for a long time
• We might unnecessarily redo transactions which have already output their updates to 
the database.
• Streamline recovery procedure by periodically performing checkpointing
•1. Output all log records currently residing in main memory onto stable storage.
•2. Output all modified buffer blocks to the disk.
•3. Write a log record < checkpoint L> onto stable storage where L is a list of all 
transactions active at the time of checkpoint.
•4. All updates are stopped while doing checkpointing
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 43

Checkpoints
•During recovery we need to consider only the most recent transaction Ti that started before 
the checkpoint, and transactions that started after Ti.
• Scan backwards from end of log to find the most recent <checkpoint L> record
• Only transactions that are in L or started after the checkpoint need to be redone or undone
• Transactions that committed or aborted before the checkpoint already have all their updates 
output to stable storage.
• Some earlier part of the log may be needed for undo operations
• Continue scanning backwards till a record <Ti start> is found for every transaction Ti in L.
• Parts of log prior to earliest <Ti start> record above are not needed for recovery, and can be 
erased whenever desired.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 44

Checkpoints
•T1 can be ignored 
(updates already output to disk 
due to checkpoint)
• T2 and T3 redone.
• T4 undone
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 45

Recovery Algorithm
•Logging (during normal operation):
• <Ti start> at transaction start
• <Ti, Xj, V1, V2> for each update, and
• <Ti commit> at transaction end
• Transaction rollback (during normal operation)
• Let Ti be the transaction to be rolled back
• Scan log backwards from the end, and for each log record of Ti of the form <Ti, Xj, V1, V2>
• Perform the undo by writing V1 to Xj,
• Write a log record <Ti , Xj, V1>
• such log records are called compensation log records
• Once the record <Ti start> is found stop the scan and write the log record <Ti abort> 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 46

Fuzzy Checkpointing
• To avoid long interruption of normal processing during checkpointing, allow updates to 
happen during checkpointing
• Fuzzy checkpointing is done as follows:
1. Temporarily stop all updates by transactions
2. Write a <checkpoint L> log record and force log to stable storage
3. Note list M of modified buffer blocks
4. Now permit transactions to proceed with their actions
5. Output to disk all modified buffer blocks in list M
oblocks should not be updated while being output
oFollow WAL: all log records pertaining to a block must be output before the block is output
6. Store a pointer to the checkpoint record in a fixed position last_checkpoint on disk
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 47

Fuzzy Checkpointing
• When recovering using a fuzzy checkpoint, start scan from the checkpoint record pointed to 
by last_checkpoint
• Log records before last_checkpoint have their updates reflected in database on disk, and 
need not be redone.
• Incomplete checkpoints, where system had crashed while performing checkpoint, are 
handled safely
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 48

ARIES
• ARIES- Algorithm for Recovery and Isolation Exploiting Semantics 
•ARIES is the most widely used database recovery algorithm in modern Database 
Management Systems (DBMS). 
• It was developed by IBM and is used in systems such as IBM Db2 and has influenced 
recovery mechanisms in many other database systems.
• Its purpose is to recover the database after a system crash while ensuring the ACID 
properties, especially Atomicity and Durability.
• It incorporates numerous optimizations to reduce overheads during normal processing and to 
speed up recovery.
• It is designed to improve concurrency, reduce logging overhead and reduce recovery time.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 49

ARIES
ARIES:
1. Uses log sequence number (LSN) to identify log records.
o Stores LSNs in pages to identify what updates have already been applied to a database page
2. Supports Physiological redo.
3. Uses Dirty page table to avoid unnecessary redos during recovery.
4. Uses Fuzzy checkpointing that only records information about dirty pages, and does not 
require dirty pages to be written out at checkpoint time.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 50

ARIES Optimizations
Physiological redo
• Affected page is physically identified, action within page can be logical
• Used to reduce logging overheads
• e.g. when a record is deleted and all other records have to be moved to fill hole
• Physiological redo can log just the record deletion
• Physical redo would require logging of old and new values for much of the page
• Requires page to be output to disk atomically
• Easy to achieve with hardware RAID, also supported by some disk systems
• Incomplete page output can be detected by checksum techniques
• But extra actions are required for recovery.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 51

ARIES Data Structures
1. Log sequence number (LSN)
2. Page LSN
3. Log records
4. Dirty page table
5. Checkpoint log record
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 52

ARIES Data Structures
Log sequence number (LSN)
• It uniquely identifies each log record.
• Must be sequentially increasing.
• Generated such that it can also locate the log record on disk.
• ARIES splits a log into multiple log files, each of which has a file number.
• The LSN then consists of a file number and an offset within the file.
• This allows fast access.
• Easily extended to handle multiple log files.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 53

ARIES Data Structures
Page LSN
• Each page maintains an identifier called the PageLSN.
• PageLSN is the LSN of the last log record whose effects are reflected on the page.
• To update a page:
• X-latch the page, and write the log record
• Update the page
• Record the LSN of the log record in PageLSN
• Unlock page
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 54

ARIES Data Structures
Page LSN
• To flush page to disk, must first S-latch page
• Thus, page state on disk is operation consistent
• Required to support physiological redo
• PageLSN is used during recovery to prevent repeated redo
• Thus, ensuring idempotence
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 55

ARIES Data Structures
Log records
• Each log record contains LSN of previous log record of the same transaction
• LSN in log record may be implicit
• Special redo-only log record called compensation log record (CLR)
• used to log actions taken during recovery that never need to be undone
• Serves the role of operation-abort log records used in earlier recovery algorithm
• Has a field UndoNextLSN to note next (earlier) record to be undone
• Records in between would have already been undone
• Required to avoid repeated undo of already undone actions
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 56

ARIES Data Structures
Log records
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 57

ARIES Data Structures
DirtyPageTable
• List of pages in the buffer that have been updated
• Contains, for each such page
• PageLSN of the page
• RecLSN is an LSN such that log records before this LSN have already been applied to the 
page version on disk
• Set to current end of log when a page is inserted into dirty page table (just before being updated)
• Recorded in checkpoints, helps to minimize redo work
• Whenever the page is flushed to disk, the page is removed from the DirtyPageTable.
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 58

ARIES Data Structures
Checkpoint log record
• Contains:
• DirtyPageTable and list of active transactions
• For each active transaction, LastLSN, the LSN of the last log record written by the 
transaction
• Fixed position on disk notes LSN of last completed checkpoint log record
• Dirty pages are not written out at checkpoint time. Instead, they are flushed out 
continuously, in the background
• Checkpoint is thus very low overhead, can be done frequently
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 59

ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 60
ARIES Data Structures

ARIES Recovery Algorithm
• ARIES recovery involves three passes:
1. Analysis pass
2. Redo pass
3. Undo pass
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 61

ARIES Recovery Algorithm
Analysis pass: determines
• Which transactions to undo
• Which pages were dirty (disk version not up to date) at time of crash
• RedoLSN: LSN from which redo should start
Redo pass
• Repeats history, redoing all actions from RedoLSN
• RecLSN and PageLSNs are used to avoid redoing actions already reflected on page 
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 62

ARIES Recovery Algorithm
Undo pass
• Rolls back all incomplete transactions
• Transactions whose abort was complete earlier are not undone
• Key idea: no need to undo these transactions: earlier undo actions were logged, and are 
redone as required
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 63

ARIES Recovery Algorithm
• Analysis, redo and undo passes
• Analysis determines where redo should start
• Undo has to go back till start of earliest incomplete transaction
ST. FRANCIS INSTITUTE OF TECHNOLOGY 64

ARIES Algorithm
Analysis pass
• Starts from last complete checkpoint log record
• Reads DirtyPageTable from log record
• Sets RedoLSN = min of RecLSNs of all pages in DirtyPageTable
• In case no pages are dirty, RedoLSN = checkpoint record’s LSN
• Sets undo-list = list of transactions in checkpoint log record
• Reads LSN of last log record for each transaction in undo-list from checkpoint log record
• Scans forward from checkpoint

ARIES Algorithm
Analysis pass
• Scans forward from checkpoint
• If any log record found for transaction not in undo-list, adds transaction to undo-list
• Whenever an update log record is found
• If page is not in DirtyPageTable, it is added with RecLSN set to LSN of the update log 
record
• If transaction end log record found, delete transaction from undo-list
• Keeps track of last log record for each transaction in undo-list
• May be needed for later undo

Analysis pass
• At end of analysis pass:
• RedoLSN determines where to start redo pass
• RecLSN for each page in DirtyPageTable used to minimize redo work
• All transactions in undo-list need to be rolled back

ARIES Algorithm
Redo pass: Repeats history by replaying every action not already reflected in the page on 
disk, as follows:
• Scans forward from RedoLSN. Whenever an update log record is found:
1. If the page is not in DirtyPageTable or the LSN of the log record is less than the 
RecLSN of the page in DirtyPageTable, then skip the log record.
2. Otherwise fetch the page from disk. If the PageLSN of the page fetched from disk is less 
than the LSN of the log record, redo the log record
NOTE: if either test is negative the effects of the log record have already appeared on the 
page. First test avoids even fetching the page from disk!

ARIES Algorithm
Undo pass
• Performs backward scan on log undoing all transaction in undo-list
• Backward scan optimized by skipping unneeded log records as follows:
• Next LSN to be undone for each transaction set to LSN of last log record for transaction 
found by analysis pass.
• At each step pick largest of these LSNs to undo, skip back to it and undo it
• After undoing a log record
• For ordinary log records, set next LSN to be undone for transaction to PrevLSN noted in 
the log record
• For compensation log records (CLRs) set next LSN to be undo to UndoNextLSN noted in 
the log record
• All intervening records are skipped since they would have been undone already

Recovery Actions in ARIES

Other ARIES Features
•Recovery Independence
• Pages can be recovered independently of others
• E.g. if some disk pages fail they can be recovered from a backup while other pages are 
being used
• Savepoints:
• Transactions can record savepoints and roll back to a savepoint
• Useful for complex transactions
• Also used to rollback just enough to release locks on deadlock

Other ARIES Features
•Fine-grained locking:
• Index concurrency algorithms that permit tuple level locking on indices can be used
• These require logical undo, rather than physical undo, as in earlier recovery algorithm
• Recovery optimizations: For example:
• Dirty page table can be used to prefetch pages during redo
• Out of order redo is possible:
• redo can be postponed on a page being fetched from disk, and performed when page is 
fetched.
• Meanwhile other log records can continue to be processed
